chief_complaint: wheezing and cough triggered by cat dander exposure
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with wheezing and cough triggered by cat dander exposure. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks breathing in heavy pet hair and dust while helping clean his friend's apartment clogged up his lungs.
concerns: He is worried that his chest tightness will force him to drop out of a weekend cycling race he trained months for.
expectations: He hopes to get an inhaler to clear his lungs and relieve the tight chest immediately.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Allergic Asthma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Allergic Asthma: ICS-Formoterol controller, Albuterol rescue inhaler, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Allergic Asthma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Non-allergic (irritant) asthma without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe breathlessness or inability to speak in full sentences.
management_principles: Plan for Allergic Asthma: ICS-Formoterol controller, Albuterol rescue inhaler
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Allergic Asthma

teaching.one_liner: Airway hyperresponsiveness triggered by inhaled allergens — such as cat dander — causing wheeze and cough on exposure.
red_flags: Severe breathlessness or inability to speak in full sentences

must_ask.say: Does the wheezing or cough happen specifically around cats or other pets?
How often does this happen, and how long do symptoms last after exposure?
Have you been diagnosed with asthma or other allergies before?
Do you use any inhalers, and do they help?
How bad does the wheezing get — can you still talk normally?

history.answer: Whenever I am around my daughter's new cat, I start wheezing, coughing, and feeling short of breath.
It started about three weeks ago, shortly after my daughter brought a cat home, and it has gradually become more noticeable.
During an episode around the cat my chest gets very tight, but otherwise I can walk and climb two flights of stairs without stopping.
It comes on in episodes when I am near the cat or inside the house and settles down when I step outside into fresh air.
No, I can lie completely flat on one pillow without any shortness of breath, and I do not wake up gasping for air at night.
Being close to the cat triggers it reliably, and cold morning air or brisk jogging also makes the coughing worse.
Yes, I hear a distinct high-pitched whistling or wheezing sound in my chest whenever I breathe out during these spells.
I have had a dry, nagging cough with a little bit of clear mucus, but I have not had any fever or chills at all.
I do not have any crushing or sharp chest pain, just an uncomfortable tightness across my chest when I wheeze.
No, my heart does not race, and I have not felt lightheaded, dizzy, or faint.
No, I have never coughed up any blood.
No, I have not noticed any swelling in my legs or ankles, and my weight has been steady.
No calf pain or swelling at all, and I have not had any recent surgeries, prolonged bed rest, or long flights.
I have been feeling unusually tired and run-down lately, but I have not had pale skin or any dark, bloody stools.
No, I have not experienced any tingling or numbness around my mouth or fingers, and I was not feeling panicked or hyperventilating.
I have never been diagnosed with asthma, chronic lung disease, or heart conditions, and I have never used an inhaler.
I have never smoked cigarettes or e-cigarettes in my entire life.
I work in an office with no chemical or dust exposures, but my daughter adopted an indoor cat about a month ago.
I do not take blood pressure medications like beta-blockers, aspirin, or any pain relievers.
I used to get mild sneezing and a runny nose during spring pollen season, but I never had asthma or eczema as a child.
I figured inhaling all that cat hair and thick dust while helping my friend move just clogged up my chest.
I've been training for months for a big cycling race this weekend, and I'm worried this wheezing will force me to pull out.
I was hoping you could give me a puff of an inhaler to open my lungs so I can breathe normally again.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter remedies, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications or foods.
I only drink socially, having a glass of wine or a beer once or twice on the weekend.
I work as an accountant at an office and live in an apartment with my wife, teenage daughter, and our new cat.
My sister has seasonal allergic rhinitis and uses an inhaler for mild asthma, but my parents do not have any lung problems.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, pulse 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Well-appearing adult male in no acute respiratory distress, speaking comfortably in full sentences with no cyanosis or accessory muscle use.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are clear without icterus.
Nasal mucosa is pale and mildly boggy with clear discharge; posterior pharynx is clear without erythema or tonsillar exudate.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy noted.
Internal jugular vein pulsation is not elevated, measuring less than 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
Symmetric chest expansion with no intercostal retractions, chest wall tenderness, or palpable thrills.
Resonant percussion notes equally bilaterally throughout both lung fields.
Mild end-expiratory high-pitched wheezing heard diffusely across bilateral lung fields; no crackles, rhonchi, or stridor.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or third heart sound.
No pretibial pitting edema noted in either lower extremity.
Calves are supple, non-tender to palpation, and symmetric without erythema, warmth, or swelling.
